issues.explanation: For a combat trauma profile, 'kids crying' is not impossible, but it is a relatively specific trigger that would usually be supported by memory or appraisal content involving civilians/children; here the memory and appraisal items do not provide that link, so this trigger is hard to integrate with the rest of the profile.

issues.item: Negative Appraisals: Physical Vulnerability: My body has been permanently damaged by what happened
issues.explanation: 'My body has been permanently damaged by what happened' implies an enduring physical injury theme, but the rest of the selected items do not support a bodily injury-focused combat presentation: memory items emphasize fragmentation/unreality, triggers emphasize intrusion/power imbalance, and strategies emphasize avoidance/hypervigilance rather than injury management. This appraisal is insufficiently anchored in the rest of the profile.

vignette:
Leilani was a curriculum designer, sixty-six years old, divorced, and living alone in a quiet suburban neighborhood. Twenty years ago, she served as a medic in a combat zone, and one memory had never loosened its grip: the sound of a medevac helicopter landing in a dust storm, rotors thudding, while she tried to keep pressure on a wound that wouldn't stop bleeding. The memory came in disconnected pieces-the hot grit on her face, the screaming, the rotor wash that made her feel like the ground was shaking-and sometimes she could not find words to describe what happened, even though she knew it was real. The story felt so extreme that she sometimes doubted it had actually happened to her, which only added to her confusion.

A helicopter flying overhead, even at a distance, would trigger the memory without warning. The sound would drop her right back into that dust storm, and in those moments she felt the familiar surge of hypervigilance, certain that she had to be on guard all the time. What frightened her most was the self-doubt that followed: she could not trust herself to do the right thing, not then, not now. She had come to believe that she was fundamentally isolated and set apart from others, that no one could understand what she carried. That conviction made her avoid going out whenever possible, and when she did leave the house-for groceries, for a doctor's appointment-she always stayed close to the exit, scanning for a way out. She was careful not to allow herself to feel any strong emotion, because she was certain that if she did, she would lose control entirely.

The avoidance itself made the memory worse. When she stayed home, the disconnected pieces of the event seemed to press in more intensely, as if her own vigilance was feeding the fragments. And the more she avoided her feelings, the more she felt isolated and unable to trust herself, which in turn made her more watchful for any sign of danger. A power imbalance-being in a situation where someone had authority over her, like a supervisor at work or a doctor in an office-could also trigger the memory, because it reminded her of the helplessness she had felt during the evacuation. That helplessness reinforced her hypervigilance and her sense of being set apart, and the cycle tightened.

At work, she had started to take on only projects that allowed her to work from home, avoiding meetings where she might feel trapped. She told herself it was efficiency, but she knew it was fear. The isolation had cost her friendships; she had stopped returning calls from old colleagues because explaining why she felt so different seemed impossible. What finally brought her to seek help was a moment in a parking lot: a delivery truck's reverse beeping sounded like a warning siren, and she found herself on the ground, heart pounding, unable to breathe. She was afraid that she was losing her mind, and more than anything, she wanted to stop feeling so alone in it.
